21660-an-introduction-to-the-industrial-:
Edward P. Cheyney introduces England's working past in An Introduction to the Industrial and Social History of England, issued in 1901. The British Isles, he begins, lie northwest of Europe, split from it by the Channel and North Sea. At the narrowest the gap is only twenty miles.

Cheyney traces farming, towns, guilds, and trade from early times onward. A picture of Gidea Hall in Essex shows a new manor amid open fields. The book aimed at students meeting economic history as a set subject. Its clear, plain survey helped fix that subject in schools on both sides of the Atlantic.

the-evolution-of-an-empire-a-brief-histo:
Mary Parmele's The Evolution of an Empire gives a brief sketch of English history. Her preface owns the hard task: a vast picture with crowds of figures must fit a small canvas. She aims to trace the streams that feed England's life today, and to mark where its laws, courts, and customs began. Two threads, she says, weave through all: religion and money.

Kings taxed, folk resisted, and faith shifted power. Parmele wrote many such short histories for home study. Her clear thread makes a first map of England's growth from Saxon roots to her own close of century.
the-evolution-of-dodd-a-pedagogical-stor:
William Hawley Smith's The Evolution of Dodd, dated by its title page to 1897, calls itself a pedagogical story of the survival of the fittest. Its mottoes hold that social forms are made for man, not man for them, and that creation's chief aim is the growth of the single soul. Chapter one opens with joy in the Weaver house at the birth of a boy, the first of his line.

A father feels his manhood sealed by the word father. Dodd's schooling, scrapes, and slow making fill the tale. Smith, a school man, argues that boys grow by nature, not by moulds.
